title: AIDA review record
description: What one pass of the review stage found, at <task folder>/review/review.json (ideal/review.md, 'The review record'). One file per task, in its own folder beside research/, design/ and implementation/, because implementation's own `restart` archives that folder whole and a review inside it would go with a build restart it has nothing to do with. Four actions write it in turn: `checks` creates it with the change set and checks 3 to 8, `findings` adds checks 2, 9 to 12 and 16 and every finding, `surfaces` adds checks 13 to 15 and the surface rows, and `close` adds check 1, the criterion verdicts and the verdict. A re-run archives the previous record to review/review-<date>-<commit>.json before it writes, and refuses when that move fails (exit 63). Plain JSON, no fences, no markdown. A field present in a real record but absent from this schema's `properties` is a defect in the schema, not a value to silently accept, which is why `additionalProperties` is false.

schemaVersion.description: The shape this file was written in, the same field every other AIDA record carries.

takenAt.description: The UTC date this record was first written, YYYY-MM-DD. Set by the script, never typed by hand.

task.description: The task's own id, read from task.json. Joined on, never re-minted.

reviewedRange.description: The change set, copied from `commitRange` in implementation/finished.json. Review computes none of its own, because a second producer for one fact is what foundations.md forbids. An empty range is a real state: the two commits are then equal, and the report says so rather than the record hiding it.

reviewedAt.description: The commit the review read, which is the code repository's HEAD when `checks` ran and the right-hand end of the range above. `checks` refuses a dirty working tree (exit 61), so this value describes a tree nothing uncommitted changes. Every later action refuses when the code path has moved off it or gone dirty (exit 51), because a finding about code that is no longer there is not a finding.

runMode.description: Copied from the ledger, which copied it from the task when the build started. It decides who may answer: a person's answer is accepted only when a person is present, so `surfaces` refuses --accept-baseline and `close` refuses --row on an autonomous run (exit 70, the number tests-freeze already gives that refusal).

recipes.description: One row per framework the project declares, written by `checks`. It holds the two recipe paths that run resolved to, or the word for the lookup that failed. `surfaces` reads the check recipe path from here rather than taking a flag, so the surface block is read from the same file the tool rows came from and review keeps its two lookups.

checks.description: One row per check, in the order the actions record them. The sixteen checks carry the ids every-criterion, non-goals, serves-a-criterion, test-and-mutation, coding-standards, static-analysis, security, suite, solid, dry, architecture-fit, guides, e2e, visual-regression, visual-parity and framework-practices. The list is longer than sixteen whenever a check recipe declares a tool row beyond the three named above: the block is a floor, not the list, and every row it declares is run and recorded here (ideal/review.md, 'The check commands block is not fixed at three rows').

criteria.description: One row per criterion in the frozen contract, written by `close`. The same verdicts are written back into alignment.json, which is the only field review writes into the contract.

findings.description: Every finding the architecture reviewer raised, written by `findings`. An empty list is a real state and it is what a clean review looks like. Review acts on none of them: it records each one with its disposition and hands the record to a person.

surfaces.description: One row per surface the registry holds, written by `surfaces`. Empty when no registry is recorded or no kind is enabled, which is a project with no surfaces rather than a project whose surfaces passed.

surfaceSetup.description: What `surfaces` found about setting the surfaces up. `registered` is a project that already has a registry. `available` is a framework whose recipe carries surface rows that are not absent while the project has no registry, which is when the skill offers setup once. `not-offered-autonomous` is the same state with nobody present to ask. `not-applicable` is a framework that declares every surface row absent. A refusal a person gives is not kept here, because no field outside this task holds one; the offer is therefore made again on the next task, and that is recorded in deferred-changes.md rather than worked around here.

mutation.description: What the `mutation` row of the test-execution recipe found over the changed files, written by `checks`. A recipe with no such row leaves this undeclared, never met: decision 5 separates the order a test was written in from its power to fail, and a score nobody measured proves nothing about the second.

verdict.description: The four words every check in this stage uses, for the mutation row's own run.

detail.description: Why that verdict, naming the framework and what the run printed or why it did not run.

score.description: The score as the tool printed it: the first output line naming a score, copied verbatim and never parsed into a number, because each of the four tools prints its own shape and a number this script derived would be a fifth. Empty when no row ran, and empty when the run named no score.

survivors.description: Every surviving mutant the run reported. The reviewer reads these as one more lens, and a survivor inside code a criterion covers becomes a finding citing that criterion.

output.description: What the mutation command printed, standard output and standard error together. Present only when a command ran.

exitCode.description: What the mutation command exited with. Present only when a command ran.

verdict.description: The review's own outcome, written by `close` and absent until then. Two words, not three: a check reading unmet fails, a check reading unknown fails, met and undeclared both pass, and a criterion reading unmet or unanswered means no sign off whatever the checks said. The rows say which check or criterion caused a fail. An absent verdict is a review that has not closed, never a review that passed.

catalogNotes.description: What this review saw about the catalog, one line each: a guide the code contradicts, a recipe whose command no longer runs, a pattern the framework wants and no guide names. Review writes nothing to the catalog. A person decides whether a note becomes a proposal, and `close` names the count so the evidence is not lost in silence.

framework.description: The framework name as project.json records it.

testRecipe.description: The test-execution recipe path this run read for that framework, as the caller handed it over. Empty when the lookup failed.

checkRecipe.description: The review recipe path this run read for that framework. Empty when the lookup failed. `surfaces` reopens this file for its `## Surface commands` block.

testRecipeSha256.description: A sha256 over the test-execution recipe this run read, or empty when the lookup failed. Recorded the way baseline.json records its own, so a reader can tell a recipe that changed between the build and the review from one that did not.

checkRecipeSha256.description: A sha256 over the review recipe this run read, or empty when the lookup failed. `checks` refuses (exit 73) when this is not the hash the baseline recorded for the same framework, because checks 5 to 7 subtract that baseline and the subtraction is only honest while both runs read the same file.

lookup.description: How the lookup answered. The three failures stay apart because only the first says anything about the framework: no recipe records that framework's checks undeclared, while an unreachable listing and a failed fetch record them unknown, since nobody looked. Collapsing the two writes a false finding nothing can tell from a true one.

id.description: Which check this is. The sixteen ids are listed in this schema's own `checks` description; a tool row the recipe declares beyond the three named tools carries the row's own id, because the ids are open.

verdict.description: The same four words the build record uses, and build-record-schema.json is the authority for them. `undeclared` means nothing declared a command for this check, or the recipe declared that row absent, or the row did not apply to the changed files; it is never satisfied and never a pass, and it does not fail the review. `unknown` means nothing this check reads could be read, and it does fail the review. A check with two inputs that got one answers from that one and names what it did not get.

detail.description: Why this verdict, in plain words naming what was compared: an exit code, a file that matched no order, a marker that was found, or the lens that returned nothing.

absent.description: True when the recipe row for this check was declared absent, and `detail` carries the recipe's own reason. It exists because undeclared covers two facts that must not read alike: a framework saying it has no such tool answered the question, and a caller that passed no recipe answered nothing.

exitCode.description: What the command exited with. Present only on a check that ran one.

output.description: What the command printed. Present only on a check that ran one. Check 1 reads the suite check's own output here, comparing test names as text.

framework.description: The framework whose recipe carried this row. Present only on a check that ran a command. One tool row may carry a command from one framework only: two frameworks each declaring one refuses before any check runs (exit 72).

id.description: The criterion id scope minted. Joined on, never the criterion's text.

verifiedBy.description: Copied from the frozen contract, so a reader never has to look the criterion back up to know why a verdict is unanswered.

verdict.description: The contract's own three words, from alignment-schema.json, which reserves this field for the review. Three and not four: a criterion nobody could reach is not the same as one that failed, and `unanswered` is never a pass. This same value is written back into alignment.json.

answeredBy.description: Who answered. `script` for a machine-verified criterion joined against the suite result, `person` for a checklist row a person read, `nobody` for a row an unattended run could not put to anyone. A run with nobody present cannot sign off a task carrying one person-verified criterion, and this field is what makes that visible.

id.description: The finding's own id, `f` followed by a number with no leading zero, minted by the reviewer in its own findings file and joined on here.

lens.description: Which of the seven lenses raised it. One dispatch carries all seven, and each of checks 2, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 16 reads its verdict off its own lens: met when that lens returned nothing, unmet when it returned a finding. The `mutation` lens is the survivors read, and it lands on check 4.

severity.description: How bad the reviewer judged it. The three words are already in agents/reviewer.md and finished-schema.json, and this is that same vocabulary rather than a fourth. A high-severity security fault citing neither a criterion nor a non-goal is raised at once rather than queued, because leaving it queued ships it.

file.description: Where the finding is, as the reviewer wrote it, relative to codePath. May be empty: a finding about something absent has no file to name.

lines.description: Which lines, as the reviewer wrote it. A string rather than two numbers, because a reviewer writes a range, a list or a single number and none of the three is worth normalizing for a reader.

linkedTo.description: The one criterion id or non-goal id this finding cites, or empty when it cites neither. Empty is the third case of the classifier and is what `disposition` then records.

evidence.description: What the reviewer saw. Required, because a finding with nothing to read is not a finding. A reason in a builder's report never lowers it: those reports are refused as authority.

disposition.description: What this finding is. `criterion` means this task's work, and that criterion reads unmet. `non-goal` means this task did what it said it would not do. `follow-up` is a finding citing neither, which becomes a task a person creates: review records it and names it in the report, whatever the run mode, because the only producer of a task interviews a person. Folding such a finding in silently is what scope exists to prevent.

id.description: The surface's own id, from the registry. Joined on, never re-minted.

verdict.description: What this surface came to. A registry surface with no result reads unmet, because a gate that cannot notice its subject going absent cannot inform. A run that selected nothing reads unknown, which is version 5's own comment on its end-to-end gate: zero tests ran is never a pass.

ran.description: Whether a command ran for this surface at all.

walked.description: Whether a person looked at this surface, at every viewport, including when it passed. Version 5 measured why: an aggregate moved from 37 percent to 28 percent while six visible defects sat inside the passing surfaces. False on an unattended run, and checks 13 to 15 then read unknown.

reportPath.description: Where the harness wrote its own report, when it names one. Empty otherwise.

baselineAccepted.description: True when a person accepted a new baseline for this surface in this review. Accepted in two stages, plan then write, and never on an unattended run.

text.description: One surviving mutant, the line the tool printed, copied verbatim. The four tools print four shapes, so this is the tool's own words and never a shape this script imposed.

file.description: The file the line named, when the line named one. Empty otherwise.

criterion.description: The criterion whose frozen tests cover that file, when one does. Empty otherwise, and a survivor with no criterion is still recorded: the reviewer reads the list, and a survivor nobody can attach is a fact rather than a finding.

seen.description: What was seen, in one line.

where.description: Where it was seen: a recipe path and its row, a guide path, or the check that noticed.
